issues.legal_issue: An adoption is not invalid merely because the deed records the mother’s consent when the living father and mother jointly gave the child in adoption.
material_facts: The child’s father was alive when the adoption took place.
Oral evidence accepted by the lower courts showed that both parents gave the child in adoption.
The adoption deed stated that the child’s parents gave him in adoption and separately recorded the mother’s thumb-mark as a token of her consent.
The challenge alleged that the adoption was invalid because the mother, rather than the living father, had given the child in adoption.
issues.conclusion: The adoption was not invalid on the ground that the mother alone gave the child in adoption; the evidence established that both parents gave him in adoption, and the mother’s recorded consent did not show otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 6 and 9(2) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, a living father has the right to give a child in adoption, but may not exercise that right without the mother’s consent. A deed stating that the parents gave the child in adoption, together with a separate record of the mother’s consent, does not establish that the mother alone gave the child in adoption.

issues.definition: When a challenge based on who gave the child in adoption arises in a case with these facts, the adoption is not invalid on the ground that the mother alone gave the child in adoption.

issues.legal_issue: A child adopted by a widow becomes the adopted child of her deceased husband as well as of the widow.
material_facts: A man died before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force, leaving a widow and property.
After the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 came into force, the widow adopted a child whose natural parents were living.

After the widow died, the nearest reversioner of her deceased husband challenged the adoption and argued that the adopted child was the widow’s son alone and could not succeed to the husband’s property.
The lower courts held that the adoption was valid and that the adopted child was entitled to succeed to the deceased husband’s property in preference to the claimant.
issues.conclusion: The adopted child was, in effect, the adopted son of the widow’s deceased husband as well as of the widow, and the argument that he could not succeed to the husband’s property was rejected. The statutory restriction against divesting an estate already vested before adoption does not alter that conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5(1) and 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 contemplate adoption both by and to a Hindu. Under section 12, the adopted child’s ties in the birth family are replaced by ties in the adoptive family; because a married woman belongs to her husband’s family, a child adopted by her as a widow becomes a member of that family and is, in effect, the adopted child of her deceased husband. Section 12(c) limits an adopted child’s ability to divest an estate vested in another before adoption, and section 13 preserves the adoptive parent’s power to dispose of property; those restrictions do not imply that a child adopted by a widow is not also the adopted child of her deceased husband. The Court rejected the contrary interpretation in Nara Hanumantha Rao v. Nara Hanumayya, while recognizing that the result there was consistent with the rule against divesting an estate already vested before adoption.

issues.definition: When a succession dispute involves a child adopted by a widow after her husband’s death and the child joins the widow’s family, the child is treated as the deceased husband’s adopted son.
